newsitem.title: USA: Dole caps political journey with vote in hometown.
newsitem.headline: Dole caps political journey with vote in hometown.

text.p: After a marathon campaign that ended in the small hours of Tuesday morning, Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole cast his ballot in the town he calls the wellspring of his political values.

On a balmy autumn day in the central Kansas plains, Dole voted shortly after noon at the flag-and-bunting decked First Christian Church in his hometown of Russell. Several dozen townspeople gathered outside to watch their native son.
"I've voted before here lots ... but never voted for myself for president. I was a little nervous," Dole said after he and his wife, Elizabeth, cast their ballots.

Before voting, he identified himself to election officials, telling them "My name's Bob Dole." One official, LaRue Covalt, carefully recited the spelling of his name. "Dole. D-O-L-E. Robert. R-O-B-E-R-T."
Dole entered the voting booth, filled out an old-fashioned paper ballot, then handed it to election clerk Fara Popp, who dropped it into a metal box.
Dole has repeatedly cited the town as the source of bedrock values on which his political career was based.

At his final campaign stop hours earlier in Independence, Missouri, Dole said those values would carry him to an upset victory polls have said he would be denied. He said that in casting his vote in Russell, "I will know that this campaign has been rooted in the most important American ideals: duty, honour, country and integrity."
"The tide of this election, I believe, was turned in diners and bowling alleys, in the heart of a people where the old values endure," he said.

Dole wrapped up a 96-hour, non-stop "march to victory" in Independence before a courthouse statue of Harry Truman, the Democrat who pulled off one of America's greatest political upsets when he defied opinion polls to defeat Republican Tom Dewey in 1948.
"What was true for Harry Truman in 1948 will be true for Bob Dole and Jack Kemp in 1996," the 73-year-old former senator from Kansas said.
Election eve surveys gave Clinton leads ranging from about seven percentage points in a Reuters poll to 18 in a CBS/New York Times survey, with most in-between.

In Dole's last campaign swing, which began on Friday, he made 29 stops in 19 states, covering 10,534 miles (16,950 km). He kept up a breakneck pace around the clock, stopping for only a few hours of sleep in his last-ditch bid to defeat Clinton. He was to return to Washington to await the returns.

Before travelling to Russell from Kansas City, Dole told reporters he had reflected on the campaign as it drew to a close. "It's unique, obviously, and exciting in a way, and I'll be proud to cast my vote. I've worked pretty hard and I'm honoured to be the standard bearer for the party. It's a great responsibility and challenge. I think about all those things."
At times, the grueling pace seemed to exhaust Dole, but at other times he bounced back to deliver a vigorous speech, dance with his wife or just revel in the enthusiasm of crowds.
Sen. John McCain of Arizona, a steady travelling companion on the campaign trail, offered an emotional tribute at a rally after midnight on Tuesday in a Des Moines bowling alley.

"This is the last crusade of a great warrior, a member of a generation of Americans who went out and made the world safe for democracy so that we could have lives that were far better for ourselves and for our children," McCain said as Dole stood nearby, appearing choked up by the remarks.

McCain said the people of Russell, who contributed to pay for Dole's surgery after he suffered crippling wounds in the Second World War, made it possible for Dole to recover and serve his country. "Those were good people, the people of Russell Kansas, and he sees their faces every day," he said.

"And what we can do tomorrow is make sure that we allow Bob Dole to make that final repayment of that debt to the people of Russell, Kansas, and send him to the White House and elect him president of the United States."
